title: Husn vs Jira dashboards
metaDescription: How Husn differs from Jira's built-in dashboards. Jira dashboards count issues inside Jira. Husn reads Jira, Slack, and docs together and tells you what changed and why.
heroSubheadline: Jira dashboards are good at showing the state of issues inside Jira. Husn reads Jira alongside Slack and your documents and reasons across them, so you get meaning rather than a count. Here is how the two differ.
primaryPain: A Jira dashboard answers the question of how many issues sit in each state, and it answers it well. The trouble is that a program does not live in Jira alone. The decision that changed the plan happened in Slack, the scope sits in a document, and a board of issue counts cannot tell you that a number moved because the work slipped or because someone closed stale tickets.
painBullets: Jira dashboards only see Jira, so a dependency that lives in Slack or a doc never shows up on the board.
Gadgets report counts and burndowns, but a count rarely tells you the reason a number moved or whether it matters.
Each board has to be built and tuned by hand, so the view reflects how someone set up the gadgets, not the current risk.
whyHardHeading: Why a Jira board stops short
whyHard: A dashboard inside one tool can only reflect that tool, so cross system context, where most risk actually lives, is invisible to it.
Issue counts and velocity charts describe motion, not meaning, so you still have to open tickets and read threads to learn what is going on.
Gadgets are configured once and rarely revisited, so the board slowly drifts from the questions the program is now facing.
howHusnHelps: Husn reads Jira, Slack, and docs together, so it sees the dependency or decision that a Jira only board cannot.
It tells you what changed, why it matters, and who is affected, and traces every point back to the ticket, message, or document it came from.
There are no gadgets to build. Husn reasons across the work and surfaces the risks that matter now, not the ones a board was tuned for last quarter.

faq.q: Does Husn replace our Jira dashboards?
faq.a: It does not have to. Many teams keep their Jira boards for issue level tracking and use Husn for the cross tool picture, the reasons behind the numbers, and the risks that span Slack and docs.

faq.q: Can Husn see things outside Jira?
faq.a: Yes. That is the main difference. Husn reads Jira, Slack, and your documents together, so it surfaces dependencies and decisions that never make it onto a Jira board.

faq.q: Is this just a smarter Jira gadget?
faq.a: No. A gadget displays what is in Jira. Husn reasons across Jira, Slack, and docs to tell you what changed, why, and who is affected, and traces each point to its source.

faq.q: Will Husn change anything in Jira?
faq.a: No. Husn is read only. It never creates, edits, moves, or closes anything in Jira, Slack, or your documents.

title: Husn vs manual status reports
metaTitle: Husn vs Manual Status Reports | Husn
metaDescription: How Husn differs from writing status reports by hand. A hand written report carries real judgment but is slow and from memory. Husn reads the work and drafts it for you.
heroSubheadline: A status report written by hand carries something a tool cannot fake, the judgment of someone who knows the program. The cost is the hours it takes and the gaps memory leaves. Husn reads the work and drafts the report, so the judgment is yours to apply, not to assemble from scratch.
primaryPain: Writing a status report by hand is one of the most expensive habits in delivery. Someone spends part of a day reconstructing the week from memory and a dozen open tabs, and by the time the report is sent it is already a little out of date. The judgment in it is real and worth having, but it is wrapped in hours of low value assembly.
painBullets: A hand written report is built from memory and a quick scan of tools, so the items that did not come to mind simply do not appear.
It takes real time to assemble, time the writer would rather spend on the work the report is about.
By the time it is written and circulated, the situation has often moved on, so the reader acts on a stale picture.
whyHard: Memory is selective under time pressure, so a report reflects what was top of mind, not necessarily what mattered most.
The assembly work competes with delivery, so reports get rushed, skipped, or delegated to whoever has an hour free.
A snapshot written on Thursday describes Thursday, and the reader usually opens it after the situation has changed again.
howHusnHelps: Husn reads Jira, Slack, and docs and drafts the report from the work itself, so nothing relevant is left out because someone forgot it.
It does the assembly, so the writer's time goes to judgment and decisions rather than gathering and formatting.
Every point traces to its source, so the reader can trust the draft and the writer can edit with confidence rather than rebuild from nothing.

title: Husn vs spreadsheet project tracking
metaTitle: Husn vs Spreadsheet Project Tracking | Husn
metaDescription: How Husn differs from tracking projects in a spreadsheet. A spreadsheet is flexible and familiar but manual and stale. Husn reads the work and keeps the picture current.
heroSubheadline: A spreadsheet bends to whatever you need it to be, which is exactly why people reach for it. The catch is that every cell is filled in by hand, so the tracker is only ever as current as the last person who updated it. Husn reads the work and keeps the picture current on its own.
primaryPain: A project tracking spreadsheet starts as the most flexible tool in the building and slowly becomes the most demanding. Every status, date, and owner is typed in by a person, so the file is accurate the day it is built and drifting by the end of the week. The flexibility that made it easy to start is the same flexibility that lets it fall out of sync without anyone noticing.
painBullets: Every row is updated by hand, so the tracker reflects who remembered to type, not what the work is actually doing.
A spreadsheet does not read Jira, Slack, or docs, so it never knows a date moved unless someone tells it.
Flexibility cuts both ways, columns and conventions drift, and the file becomes hard to trust as it grows.
whyHard: Manual entry competes with the work and loses, so the tracker is out of date within days of the last update.
A cell holds whatever was typed, with no link to the ticket or thread behind it, so you cannot tell a fresh status from an old one.
As the file grows, ownership of keeping it current blurs, and a tracker that everyone reads but no one maintains quietly stops being true.
howHusnHelps: Husn reads Jira, Slack, and docs directly, so the picture stays current without anyone updating a row.
It tells you what changed, why it matters, and who is affected, and traces every point to its source rather than to a typed in cell.
It surfaces the cross project risk a flat spreadsheet cannot model, because Husn reasons across the work instead of holding values someone entered.

title: Husn vs status meetings
metaDescription: How Husn differs from relying on status meetings to find out what changed. Meetings build alignment but are expensive and periodic. Husn reads the work between them.
heroSubheadline: A status meeting does something a document cannot, it builds alignment and trust in the room. The problem is that it is also where a roomful of people reconstruct the week out loud, on a schedule. Husn reads the work between meetings, so the time you do spend together is for decisions, not recaps.
primaryPain: Relying on the status meeting to find out what changed turns an expensive hour into a reporting cycle. Everyone gathers, each person narrates their week from memory, and the group spends most of the time getting on the same page about facts that already exist in the tools. The alignment is real and valuable, but it sits on top of a long, costly recap that did not need a meeting at all.
painBullets: A status meeting is the most expensive way to move information, a room of senior people taking turns to read out what already happened.
It runs on a cadence, so anything urgent waits for the next meeting or interrupts everyone over Slack.
The update is reconstructed from memory in the moment, so it carries the same gaps and optimism as any account told out loud.
whyHard: Synchronous time is the scarcest resource a program has, and spending it on a recap means spending it on information that did not need everyone present.
A weekly cadence sets the speed at which problems surface, so a risk that appears on Tuesday may not be discussed until the following Monday.
Verbal updates are reconstructed live, so the meeting reflects what each person recalled and chose to raise, not the full state of the work.
howHusnHelps: Husn reads Jira, Slack, and docs and surfaces what changed before the meeting, so the recap is already done when people sit down.
It does not wait for a cadence. Risks and changes surface as the work moves, so urgent items do not sit until the next slot.
It prepares a briefing traced to its source, so the meeting can spend its time on the few decisions that genuinely need the room.

Husn does not replace that, it removes the recap that fills most of the hour. If your meetings are short and decision led, keep them. If they are mostly people reading out the week, that is the gap Husn closes.
